teile.einleitung: In wartime many foods were scarce in Switzerland. So that everyone got enough, the state issued food ration cards. Only people with coupons were allowed to buy certain goods.
wichtigste: In the Second World War you needed food coupons to be allowed to buy food.
You still had to pay for the goods with money.
Rationed means: each person gets only a set amount.
From October 1942 bread was rationed too.
Heavy manual workers got larger portions.
Rationing was only completely over in July 1948.
There were already food ration cards in the First World War.

abschnitte.text: A **food ration card** had many small **coupons** printed on it. Each coupon stood for a certain amount of a product, for example sugar or butter. In the shop you handed in the coupon and could then buy the goods. But you still had to pay for them with **money**. The coupon only gave you permission to buy.

If a product is **rationed**, each person gets only a fixed share. This way what is scarce is shared out fairly. Without rationing, rich people might have bought everything up. Poor families would then have gone without. Rationing was meant to make sure that nobody had to go hungry.

In the **Second World War** Switzerland was surrounded by countries at war. Many goods could no longer be imported. Goods such as sugar were rationed early on. From July 1940 **bread** could no longer be sold fresh. Stale bread is eaten more slowly and in smaller amounts. In October **1942** bread also went onto the food ration card.

Not everyone got the same amount. People who did hard physical work needed more energy. So from 1942 **heavy manual workers** got larger portions. At the same time more vegetables, potatoes and grain were grown all over Switzerland. Fields even appeared in parks and on sports grounds. This campaign is called the **Anbauschlacht** (“battle for crops”) or the Wahlen Plan.

There were food ration cards as early as the **First World War**. From **1917** rice, sugar and then bread and flour were rationed. Later butter, cheese and milk were added. After the Second World War rationing was lifted step by step. In July **1948** it was completely over.

gewusst: Rationing in Switzerland continued for three years after the war ended.
From 1940 bread could not be sold fresh, so that people would eat less of it.

teile.einleitung: After the fall of Napoleon, Europe was reorganised at the Congress of Vienna. In 1815 the Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined the Confederation as new cantons. Switzerland now had 22 cantons.
wichtigste: In 1815 the Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined the Confederation.
This gave Switzerland 22 cantons.
From 1810 to 1813 the Valais was the French département of Simplon.
Neuchâtel was at once a canton and a principality of the King of Prussia.
Geneva received municipalities such as Carouge and Versoix.
In return Bern received the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel in the Jura.

abschnitte.text: After the fall of **Napoleon** the great powers met at the **Congress of Vienna**. They redrew the borders in Europe. Switzerland too was given a new shape. In 1815 the **Valais**, **Neuchâtel** and **Geneva** joined as new cantons. Since then Switzerland has had roughly its present borders.

**Napoleon** wanted to control the important **Simplon road** over the Alps. So in 1810 he made the Valais the French **département of Simplon**. After his fall the Valais became free. In 1815 it joined the Confederation. Its capital is **Sion** (German: Sitten), which had long been a bishop's seat.

**Neuchâtel** had a special position. It was a Swiss canton and at the same time a **principality** of the **King of Prussia**. On 1 March **1848** republicans in Neuchâtel proclaimed the **republic**. Prussia, however, did not recognise this at once. Only in **1857** did the Prussian king finally give up Neuchâtel.

**Geneva** had been annexed by **France** in 1798. It became the capital of the **département of Léman**. In 1815 Geneva joined the Confederation. But the Geneva territory was surrounded by foreign land. So it was given municipalities from **Savoy** and France, for example **Carouge** and **Versoix**. This created a link with the rest of Switzerland.

Bern had earlier ruled **Vaud** and **Aargau**. These areas had meanwhile become cantons in their own right. In compensation Bern received in 1815 most of the former **Prince-Bishopric of Basel** in the Jura. Many people there were not happy with this. Much later part of this area became the **canton of Jura**.

gewusst: Until 1848 one Swiss canton had a king as its prince: Neuchâtel.
At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Switzerland's neutrality was also recognised.

teile.einleitung: Dormant assets are bank deposits whose owners have not been in touch for a long time. In the 1990s there was a major debate about them. It was about accounts of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks.
wichtigste: Dormant assets are accounts with no contact with the owner.
In the 1990s the debate was mainly about accounts of Holocaust victims.
The World Jewish Congress pushed the debate strongly forward.
From 1996 the Volcker Commission had millions of accounts checked.
In 1997 the security guard Christoph Meili saved documents from destruction.
In 1998 UBS and Credit Suisse reached a settlement for 1.25 billion dollars.

abschnitte.text: A bank account is **dormant** when the bank no longer has contact with the owner. Perhaps he has died, and his heirs know nothing about the account. In the **Second World War** many persecuted people brought their money to Switzerland. Many of them were murdered in the **Holocaust**. Their families were often later unable to get the money back because proof was missing.

In the **1990s** the subject became known worldwide. The **World Jewish Congress** under Edgar Bronfman demanded clarification and the return of the money. It was supported by the US senator **Alfonse D'Amato**. In the USA those affected filed **class actions** against Swiss banks. In a class action many people sue together.

There was heated discussion in Switzerland. At the end of 1996 the President of the Confederation, **Jean-Pascal Delamuraz**, spoke of “blackmail” in connection with the demands. This caused outrage, and he later apologised. The Swiss ambassador in the USA, **Carlo Jagmetti**, had written of a “war” in an internal report. When the paper became public he resigned in January 1997.

In January 1997 **Christoph Meili** was working as a security guard at the Swiss Bank Corporation. In the shredding room he found old documents from the time of the Second World War. They were due to be destroyed. Meili took them with him and handed them to a **Jewish organisation**. The case caused a great stir internationally.

From **1996** the **Volcker Commission**, led by the former US central bank chief **Paul Volcker**, searched the Swiss banks. It had millions of accounts checked and found about **54,000** accounts with a possible link to Holocaust victims. In August **1998** the big banks **UBS** and **Credit Suisse** reached an agreement with the plaintiffs. They paid **1.25 billion dollars**, and the class actions were settled.

gewusst: The Volcker Commission's checking of the accounts lasted several years.
The federal government also had Switzerland's role in the Second World War examined by an independent commission of historians, the Bergier Commission.

teile.einleitung: In 1803 six new cantons were created in Switzerland. At that time Napoleon gave Switzerland a new order with the Act of Mediation. Former subject territories and allies became cantons with equal rights.
wichtigste: In 1803 the Act of Mediation created six new cantons.
The new cantons were St Gallen, the Grisons, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud.
The Fricktal had previously belonged to Austria and went to Aargau.
Karl Müller-Friedberg is seen as the founder of the canton of St Gallen.
Before 1798 Thurgau was a common lordship.
In Ticino the capital alternated between three towns until 1878.
The coat of arms of Vaud bears the words “Liberté et Patrie”.

abschnitte.text: After the French invaded in 1798 there was a great deal of conflict in Switzerland. So in **1803** **Napoleon** gave Switzerland a new constitution, the **Act of Mediation**. Mediation means acting as a go-between. Switzerland now consisted of **19 cantons**. Six of them were new: **St Gallen, the Grisons, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud**.

The canton of **Aargau** was put together from several areas. They included the **Bernese Aargau**, the **County of Baden** and the **Free Bailiwicks**. The **Fricktal** was added too. It had long been **Habsburg-Austrian**. Aarau became the capital.

The new canton of **St Gallen** was formed from very different regions. From 1803 it was led for almost thirty years by **Karl Müller-Friedberg**. He is seen as the founding father of the canton. Before 1798 **Thurgau** was a **common lordship**, that is, a subject territory of several Confederate states. Its capital became **Frauenfeld**, where the bailiff had sat earlier too.

**Ticino** too had earlier been a subject territory of the Confederates. The young canton had no fixed capital. **Bellinzona, Lugano and Locarno** took turns. Only in **1878** did Bellinzona become the permanent capital. **Vaud** had belonged to Bern until 1798. Its motto **“Liberté et Patrie”** means “Freedom and Fatherland”.

The **Grisons** had previously been an **associate state** (Zugewandter Ort), that is, an ally of the Confederates. It consisted of the **Three Leagues**: the Grey League, the League of God's House and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. In 1803 it became a full canton. To this day the Grisons is the largest canton of Switzerland by area.

gewusst: From 1798 there were no more subject territories; in 1803 several former subject territories became cantons with equal rights.
Ticino had three capitals in turn until 1878.

teile.einleitung: Marie Heim-Vögtlin was the first Swiss woman doctor. In her time almost only men were allowed to study medicine. With courage and perseverance she opened the way into this profession for women.
wichtigste: Marie Heim-Vögtlin was the first woman doctor in Switzerland.
She was born in 1845 in Bözen in the canton of Aargau.
From 1868 she studied medicine at the University of Zurich.
In 1874 she completed her studies as a doctor of medicine.
She treated mainly women and children.
Her husband Albert Heim was a well-known geologist.
In 1901 she founded a nursing school with a hospital together with other women.

abschnitte.text: Marie Vögtlin was born in **1845** in **Bözen** in the canton of **Aargau**. Her father was the **pastor** there. In those days girls were mainly supposed to learn how to run a household. Studying was almost impossible for women. But Marie wanted to learn more and help sick people.

Anyone who wants to become a doctor has to study **medicine**. Marie Vögtlin began her studies at the **University of Zurich** in **1868**. Zurich admitted women as students quite early. Many people thought this was improper at the time. Marie did not let herself be discouraged. She was the first Swiss woman to study medicine there.

In **1874** she became a **doctor of medicine**. Afterwards she opened her own **practice** in Zurich. That was something completely new at the time. In her practice she helped mainly **women and children**. Many patients were glad to be treated by a woman.

Marie Vögtlin married **Albert Heim**. He studied mountains and rocks and was a well-known **geologist** in Zurich. From then on she was called **Marie Heim-Vögtlin**. She carried on working as a doctor after her marriage. That was very unusual for a woman at the time.

In **1901** she helped to found the **Swiss Nursing School** with a hospital in Zurich. There women learned the profession of **nursing**. In the hospital, women doctors and nurses worked together. Marie Heim-Vögtlin died in 1916. To this day she is seen as a role model for women in medicine.

gewusst: The University of Zurich was one of the first in Europe to admit women to study.
At the time of her studies there were only very few women students at the University of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: With the alliance of 1332 a city joined the forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden for the first time. For the farmers of central Switzerland, Lucerne was the most important market and lay on the route to the Gotthard.
wichtigste: Lucerne was the first city in an alliance with the forest cantons.
The city was headed by a mayor, the Schultheiss.
At that time Lucerne belonged to the Habsburg domain.
In 1291 the Habsburgs bought Lucerne from Murbach Abbey.
Lucerne was the most important market town of the forest cantons.
Goods travelled by boat across the lake towards the Gotthard.
The Chapel Bridge was built around 1365.

abschnitte.titel: The first city in the alliance
abschnitte.text: **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden** are called the **forest cantons**. They were rural valley communities with farmers and herdsmen. With **Lucerne**, a **city** joined the alliance for the first time in 1332. A city had walls, craftsmen, traders and a market. The alliance thus linked the countryside and the city.

abschnitte.titel: From the abbey to the Habsburgs
abschnitte.text: For a long time Lucerne belonged to **Murbach Abbey** in Alsace. In **1291** the abbey sold its rights over the city to the **Habsburgs**. So Lucerne was under Habsburg rule when it made the alliance. The alliance with the forest cantons was therefore a brave step for the people of Lucerne.

At the head of Lucerne's council stood a **Schultheiss**, a kind of mayor. He led the meetings and represented the city. The title also existed in other cities such as **Bern** and **Solothurn**. The citizens of the city arranged many things themselves. Over time the council became more and more powerful.

For the forest cantons, Lucerne was the most important **market town**. There the farmers sold their **cattle**, their cheese and other goods. In return they bought **grain** and **salt**, which were lacking in the mountains. The city also lay on the **Gotthard route**. So Lucerne was very important for trade with the south.

abschnitte.titel: Across the lake to the Gotthard
abschnitte.text: There were hardly any roads along the steep lakeshore in those days. So goods were taken by **boat** across Lake Lucerne to **Flüelen**. From there they continued by **pack animals** over the Gotthard. Around 1365 the **Chapel Bridge** was built in Lucerne. It was part of the fortifications and is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is more than 650 years old.
The forest cantons also needed Lucerne for salt, which their valleys did not have.

teile.einleitung: The Neuchâtel Crisis was a dispute between Switzerland and Prussia in 1856 and 1857. It was about the question of whether Neuchâtel belonged to Switzerland or to the Prussian king. The conflict brought the country to the brink of war.
wichtigste: From 1815 Neuchâtel was a Swiss canton and at the same time a Prussian principality.
On 1 March 1848 republicans proclaimed the republic.
In September 1856 royalists occupied Neuchâtel Castle.
About 500 royalists were taken prisoner.
The Federal Assembly elected Guillaume-Henri Dufour as General.
On 26 May 1857 the Prussian king gave up Neuchâtel.

abschnitte.text: Since the **Congress of Vienna** Neuchâtel had been a Swiss **canton**. At the same time it still belonged to the **King of Prussia** as a **principality**. This double role was the root of the later conflict. On **1 March 1848** the radical-democratic **Montagnards** overthrew the royalist government. They proclaimed the **republic**. The Prussian king, however, maintained his claims.

In the night of **2 to 3 September 1856** supporters of the king occupied **Neuchâtel Castle**. They are called **royalists**. The castle was the seat of the government. The plan had been drawn up by Count Frédéric de Pourtalès-Steiger. But the republicans quickly won the castle back. About **500 royalists** were taken prisoner.

Prussia demanded the **release** of the prisoners. Switzerland wanted to free them only if the king gave up Neuchâtel. Prussia broke off diplomatic relations. On **27 December 1856** the Federal Assembly elected the experienced **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** as General. Switzerland sent troops to the **Rhine border**.

Emperor **Napoleon III** of France mediated between Switzerland and Prussia. The prisoners were released. Afterwards the great powers negotiated at a **conference in Paris**. For Switzerland, the envoy from Thurgau, **Johann Konrad Kern**, negotiated. In the treaty of **26 May 1857** King **Frederick William IV** gave up his rights to Neuchâtel.

gewusst: The Prussian king kept the title of Prince of Neuchâtel until his death in 1861, but Switzerland did not recognise this.
The Neuchâtel Crisis strengthened solidarity in the young federal state of 1848.

teile.einleitung: The National Council is the large chamber of the Swiss Parliament in Bern. Its 200 members represent the people and are elected every four years. Together with the Council of States, the National Council makes Switzerland's laws.
wichtigste: The National Council primarily represents the people.
It has 200 seats, which are shared among the cantons according to population.
Every canton has at least one seat; Zurich has the most seats.
The National Council is elected every four years, since 1919 by proportional representation.
At the first election in 1848 the National Council had 111 members.
In 1971 the first eleven women were elected to the National Council.
Parliament meets four times a year for ordinary sessions.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Parliament is called the **Federal Assembly** and consists of two chambers. The **National Council** represents the people, the **Council of States** represents the cantons. Because the National Council, with 200 members, is much bigger than the Council of States, with 46, it is also called the **large chamber**. Both chambers are equally powerful: a law only applies if both agree.

The 200 seats are shared among the cantons according to **population**. The canton of Zurich has the most seats; since the 2023 elections it has 36. But every canton has at least one seat, so Uri, Glarus and the two Appenzells, for example, each have only one member. In elections each canton forms its own **constituency**.

The National Council is elected by the people every four years; the last election was in October 2023. Since 1919 **proportional representation** has applied, so the seats are shared out in proportion to the parties' votes. Voters can cross names off a list, write names twice (**cumulating**) or add people from other lists (**panachage**). Anyone who is a Swiss citizen and at least 18 years old may vote.

Parliament meets four times a year for ordinary **sessions**, each lasting three weeks. The members of the National Council debate laws, decide on the federal budget and oversee the government. Much of the work is done in **committees**, small groups that prepare business. Together with the Council of States they also elect the Federal Council, meeting as the United Federal Assembly.

The National Council has existed since the federal state was founded in 1848; the model for the two-chamber system was the USA. At the first election in 1848 it had 111 members, and later it grew with the population. Since 1963 the number of seats has been fixed at 200. In 1971, after the introduction of **women's suffrage**, the first eleven women were elected; in 2023 the share of women was about 39 per cent.

The National Council meets in the **Federal Palace** in Bern in a large chamber with a wall painting of Lake Lucerne. Each year it elects a new president. This person chairs the meetings and is seen as the **“highest Swiss”**. The meetings are public; you can follow them from the gallery or on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of parliament that debates and votes separately.
An electoral system in which seats are shared out in proportion to the votes.
A sitting period of parliament lasting several weeks.
A group of members of parliament from the same or similar parties.
A small group of members of parliament who prepare business in depth.

gewusst: The members of the National Council are not professional politicians in the strict sense; many also have another job alongside.
The large wall painting in the National Council chamber shows the Rütli on Lake Lucerne, the place where, according to tradition, the Confederation began.

teile.einleitung: Le Corbusier was one of the most famous architects in the world. He was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds and built mainly in France. His ideas greatly changed the way people built in the 20th century.
wichtigste: Le Corbusier was an architect, painter and designer.
He was born in 1887 in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the canton of Neuchâtel.
His real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret.
He especially liked building with concrete.
Most of his buildings are in France.
He appeared on the 10-franc note of the eighth series.
On Lake Geneva he built the “Villa Le Lac” for his parents.

abschnitte.text: Le Corbusier was born in **1887** in **La Chaux-de-Fonds**. The town in the canton of Neuchâtel is known for its **watchmaking industry**. His real name was **Charles-Édouard Jeanneret**. At art school he first learned to decorate watch cases. A teacher encouraged him to become an architect. In his home town he built his first houses.

Later he moved to **Paris**. There he took the artist's name **Le Corbusier**. He lived in France for a long time and became a French citizen in 1930. Most of his buildings are in **France**. Well-known examples are the Villa Savoye near Paris and the chapel at Ronchamp. He even planned the city of Chandigarh in India.

Le Corbusier especially liked building with **concrete**. With it he could make smooth walls, flat roofs and large windows. His houses often stood on stilts so that there was free space underneath. He also invented his own system of measurement, the **Modulor**. It is based on the size of the human body.

In **Corseaux** on Lake Geneva he built a small house for his **parents**. It is called the **“Villa Le Lac”** and stands right on the shore. The house is long and narrow and has a long window with a view of the lake. Today you can visit it. There are also buildings in Geneva and Zurich that are linked to him.

In many photos Le Corbusier wears **round, dark glasses**. You can recognise him by them straight away. Switzerland honoured him on the yellow **10-franc note** of the eighth series, which was issued from 1995. Since 2016 several of his buildings have been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. The Villa Le Lac is one of them. Le Corbusier died in France in 1965.

gewusst: Le Corbusier was not only an architect, he also painted and designed furniture.
His buildings stand on three continents and some of them are UNESCO World Heritage sites.

teile.einleitung: The Colonels' Affair was a scandal in the First World War. Two senior Swiss officers passed secret information to Germany and Austria-Hungary. The case deepened the divide between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: At the centre were Colonels Karl Egli and Moritz von Wattenwyl.
They passed on secret daily bulletins of the General Staff.
The information went to the military attachés of the Central Powers.
The cryptographer André Langie set the case in motion.
In February 1916 the colonels were acquitted of criminal charges in Zurich.
General Wille punished both with 20 days of arrest each.
French-speaking Switzerland felt the verdict was far too mild.

abschnitte.text: In the **First World War** Switzerland was **neutral**. It was not allowed to favour any side in the war. Colonels **Karl Egli** and **Friedrich Moritz von Wattenwyl** worked in the **General Staff**. They passed on the secret **daily bulletins**, that is, the daily situation reports. They also passed on deciphered telegrams. In doing so they violated neutrality.

The information went to the **military attachés** of Germany and Austria-Hungary. A military attaché is an officer who works at an embassy abroad. Germany and Austria-Hungary were called the **Central Powers**. They were fighting against France, Britain and Russia. This angered above all **French-speaking Switzerland**, which was friendly towards France.

In 1915 the cryptographer **André Langie** cracked a Russian **secret code**. A cryptographer is an expert in secret writing. Langie noticed that dispatches referred to Swiss General Staff reports. He suspected **treason**. So he informed the National Councillor from Vaud, **Édouard Secretan**.

In **February 1916** the two colonels came before the **divisional court** in Zurich. The court **acquitted** them of criminal charges. The case went back to the military authorities for judgement on disciplinary matters. General **Ulrich Wille** punished both with **20 days of arrest** each. The Federal Council also removed them from their posts.

French-speaking newspapers sharply criticised the mild verdict. Many in **French-speaking Switzerland (Romandie)** saw it as proof of a **pro-German army leadership**. In German-speaking Switzerland, by contrast, the case was rather played down. This created a **crisis of confidence** in the army and the government. The **divide** between the parts of the country grew deeper.

gewusst: A code-breaker brought the scandal to light because he deciphered a Russian secret code.
The two colonels were acquitted by the court and punished only on disciplinary grounds.

teile.einleitung: Matthäus Schiner was Bishop of Sion and a cardinal. Around 1500 he was one of the most influential politicians in the Confederation. He fought with all his strength against French influence in Italy.
wichtigste: Matthäus Schiner came from the Goms in the Valais.
In 1499 he became Bishop of Sion.
Pope Julius II made him a cardinal in 1511.
In 1512 he led the Confederates to join the Holy League against France.
His great opponent in the Valais was Georg Supersaxo.
In 1519 he supported the election of Charles V as king.
He died of the plague in Rome in 1522.

abschnitte.text: Matthäus Schiner was born around **1465** in Mühlebach near Ernen in the **Goms**. At that time the Valais was divided into districts called **Zenden**. Schiner came from a simple background. He rose through the **Church**. He was clever, a good speaker and very ambitious.

abschnitte.titel: Bishop and ruler of the land
abschnitte.text: In **1499** Schiner became **Bishop of Sion**. The bishop was not only a spiritual shepherd. He was also **count and prefect of the Valais** and so a worldly ruler. The bishops traced this power back to a supposed gift from Charlemagne, the **“Carolina”**. But they were constantly quarrelling over power with the Zenden.

abschnitte.titel: Cardinal in the service of the Pope
abschnitte.text: Schiner was a determined opponent of **France**. Pope **Julius II** wanted to drive the French out of Italy. Schiner helped him to win the Confederates for the **Holy League**. For this the Pope made him a **cardinal** in **1511**. In 1512 the Confederates marched into Italy in the **Pavia Expedition**. The same Pope had founded the **Swiss Guard** in 1506.

**Georg Supersaxo** was a powerful politician in the Valais. At first he helped Schiner onto the bishop's throne. Later he changed to the **French camp**. The two became bitter enemies. Their struggle for power divided the Valais for many years. At times Schiner even had to flee from the Valais.

After the defeat at **Marignano** in 1515 Schiner continued his fight against France. In **1519** he supported the election of the Habsburg **Charles V** as King of the Romans and Germans. Charles was elected against the French king Francis I. After the death of Pope Leo X, Schiner stayed in **Rome**. There he died in **1522** of the **plague**.

gewusst: At one point Schiner was even talked about as a possible pope.
The Pope who made Schiner a cardinal also founded the Swiss Guard.

teile.einleitung: Maggi is a well-known brand of soups, stock and seasoning. It was founded by the Swiss man Julius Maggi. He wanted to make quick and nourishing meals possible for factory workers.
wichtigste: Julius Maggi was born in Frauenfeld in 1846.
He founded the company Maggi.
The factory stood in Kemptthal near Winterthur.
He made his first soup powders from pulses.
He wanted cheap, nourishing food for factory workers.
In 1908 the Maggi stock cube came onto the market.
Maggi seasoning has been sold in a brown bottle since 1886.

abschnitte.text: **Julius Maggi** was born in **1846** in **Frauenfeld** in the canton of Thurgau. Later he took over a **mill**. In the age of industrialisation many people worked in factories. They had long working days, little time and little money. Julius Maggi wanted to help them eat well.

For his first **soup powders** Maggi used flour made from **peas, beans and lentils**. These **pulses** are rich in **protein** and fill you up. The soups were cheap and quick to cook. So even **factory workers** could eat a warm and nourishing meal. The idea went down well at the time.

**Maggi seasoning** has existed since **1886**. A few drops give soups and other dishes more flavour. The seasoning comes in a **brown bottle** with a yellow and red label. This bottle has remained almost unchanged to this day. Many people recognise it straight away.

In **1908** the **Maggi stock cube** came onto the market. You dissolve it in hot water and get a **bouillon**, that is, a clear broth. The cube is small, keeps for a long time and is easy to transport. It became a great success all over the world.

Julius Maggi's factory stood in **Kemptthal** near Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. Many people worked there. The company grew quickly and also built factories abroad. Julius Maggi died in 1912. Later the company became part of the **Nestlé** group.

gewusst: The Maggi bottle has looked almost the same for more than 100 years.
Maggi began with soups made from peas, beans and lentils.

teile.einleitung: Mobilisation means that a country calls up its army and makes it ready to fight. In Switzerland general wartime mobilisation began on 2 September 1939, shortly after the German attack on Poland. Hundreds of thousands of men left their families and jobs and did active service until 1945 to protect the country.
wichtigste: At the end of August 1939 the Federal Council first called up the border troops.
General wartime mobilisation began on 2 September 1939.
About 430,000 soldiers and a further 200,000 or so auxiliary service personnel were called up.
In the Women's Auxiliary Service over 20,000 women at times served voluntarily.
Swiss soldiers did on average about 800 days of active service.
From 1940 the wage and income compensation scheme replaced the lost wages of the men serving.
About 4,000 Swiss soldiers died during active service.

abschnitte.text: In a **mobilisation** an army's soldiers are called away from civilian life to serve. Switzerland has a **militia army**, so the soldiers normally work in their jobs and only report for periods of service. In an emergency they have to appear at their assembly points within a short time. Switzerland had already mobilised its army in the First World War in 1914, at that time under General Ulrich Wille.

As war threatened, the Federal Council first called up the **border troops** at the end of August 1939. On 30 August 1939 the Federal Assembly elected **Henri Guisan** as General. On 2 September 1939, one day after the German attack on Poland, general wartime mobilisation began. About 430,000 soldiers reported for duty, and about 200,000 auxiliary service personnel were added.

In 1939 the **Women's Auxiliary Service** (FHD) was founded, in which at times over 20,000 women worked voluntarily for the army. They worked, for example, as radio operators, cooks or in aircraft spotting. At home, women, children and older people had to take over the men's work on farms and in shops. From 1940 the **wage and income compensation scheme** replaced the lost wages of the men serving. It is seen as the forerunner of the AVS (old-age insurance).

In May and June 1940 German aircraft repeatedly violated Swiss airspace. In the process the Swiss **air force** shot down 11 German aircraft and lost 3 of its own. Germany reacted with sharp protests and threats. On 20 June 1940, under German pressure, General Guisan forbade the air force to fight air battles over Switzerland.

After the defeat of France in 1940 part of the troops were released again. After that the army kept up its strength mostly through about 80 **partial mobilisations**, in which units relieved each other. On 25 July 1940, at the **Rütli Report**, Guisan explained to his officers the strategy of the **Réduit**, a defence in the Alps. On average each soldier did about 800 days of active service.

During active service from 1939 to 1945 about 4,000 Swiss soldiers died, mainly in accidents and from illness. For **treason**, 17 Swiss were sentenced to death and executed. Active service ended on 20 August 1945. For many families the time of mobilisation was a formative memory of hardship and solidarity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Calling up the army so that it is ready for action.
Military service in an emergency, when the country is under threat.
An army of citizens who do military service alongside their jobs.
The defensive position of the Swiss army in the Alps in the Second World War.
Service for people who did not fight as soldiers but supported the army.

gewusst: Switzerland only has a general in wartime or in times of great danger; Henri Guisan was one of only four generals in the history of the federal state.
The wage compensation scheme of 1940 was so successful that it served as a model for the AVS (old-age insurance) of 1948.

teile.einleitung: The Matterhorn near Zermatt is one of the best-known mountains in the world. Its first ascent in 1865 was a great success and at the same time a tragic accident. It was also in this period that tourism began in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The Matterhorn was first climbed on 14 July 1865.
The roped party was led by the Englishman Edward Whymper.
The group climbed from Zermatt via the Hörnli Ridge.
On the descent four of the seven climbers were killed.
Three days later Jean-Antoine Carrel reached the summit from the Italian side.
In 1863 the Swiss Alpine Club was founded in Olten.
In 1871 the Rigi Railway ran as the first rack railway in Europe.

abschnitte.text: The **Matterhorn** stands on the border between Switzerland and Italy. For a long time it was thought to be almost impossible to climb. The Englishman **Edward Whymper**, an illustrator and mountaineer, tried several times without success. His rival was the mountain guide **Jean-Antoine Carrel** from Valtournenche in Italy. Both were determined to be the first.

On **14 July 1865** a roped party of **seven** climbers reached the summit. They climbed from **Zermatt** via the **Hörnli Ridge**. This ridge is now the normal route from the Swiss side. It starts at the **Hörnli Hut** at 3,260 metres. Shortly before the summit Whymper and his guide unroped and hurried up first.

On the way down, **four** men fell down the north face: Croz, Hadow, Hudson and Douglas. The **rope** to the other three broke. So Whymper and two mountain guides survived. The accident became known all over Europe. The date is seen as the end of the **“Golden Age”** of alpinism, in which many great Alpine peaks were climbed for the first time.

Only **three days** after the first ascent, **Jean-Antoine Carrel** also reached the summit. He climbed from Italy via the **Lion Ridge**. For years he had competed with Whymper for the first victory on the summit. Today there are several routes up the Matterhorn.

In this period the Alps became more and more popular with travellers. In **1863** the **Swiss Alpine Club** was founded in **Olten**. It built huts and promoted the exploration of the mountains. In **1871** the **Rigi Railway** ran from Vitznau as the first rack railway in Europe. In **St Moritz** the hotelier **Johannes Badrutt** invited English summer guests in 1864 to come back in winter. This was the start of **winter tourism**.

gewusst: Badrutt promised his guests sunshine in winter, and the guests stayed until Easter.
The Matterhorn is about 4,478 metres high.

teile.einleitung: Niklaus von Flüe, known as Brother Klaus, lived in Obwalden in the 15th century. He was a farmer and father of a family and later became a hermit. Many people in Switzerland revere him to this day.
wichtigste: Niklaus von Flüe is called Brother Klaus.
He was born in 1417 in Flüeli near Sachseln in what is now the canton of Obwalden.
With his wife Dorothee he had ten children.
He lived as a hermit in a cell in the Ranft.
It is handed down that he ate nothing for about 19 years.
He was canonised in 1947.
He is regarded as the patron saint of Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Farmer and father of a family
abschnitte.text: **Niklaus von Flüe** was born in **1417** in **Flüeli** near Sachseln. This is in what is now the canton of **Obwalden**. He was a respected **farmer** and also held offices in his home region, for example as a judge. With his wife **Dorothee Wyss** he had **ten children**. From an early age prayer was very important to him.

abschnitte.titel: The path to becoming a hermit
abschnitte.text: At about 50 years of age Niklaus left his family to live as a **hermit**. A hermit withdraws from other people to live quietly and to **pray**. His wife Dorothee agreed to this. From then on people called him **Brother Klaus**. It was a big step for the whole family.

Brother Klaus lived in a small **cell** in the **Ranft**. This is a gorge near Flüeli, not far from his former home. Beside the cell stands a chapel. It is handed down that he ate nothing for about **19 years**. Many people came to him to ask for advice.

Brother Klaus was known for his wise advice. In 1481 a serious quarrel threatened among the Confederates. At the **Federal Diet in Stans** a priest brought a message from Brother Klaus. Afterwards the states agreed on the **Covenant of Stans**. For this reason Brother Klaus is regarded as a **peacemaker**. He died in 1487.

abschnitte.titel: Saint and patron saint of the country
abschnitte.text: In **1947** Pope **Pius XII** declared Brother Klaus a **saint**. The Catholic Church reveres him as the **patron saint** of Switzerland, that is, as the protector of the country. Many Protestants also respect him. Every year many people make a pilgrimage to Flüeli-Ranft.

gewusst: Brother Klaus lived only a few minutes away from his former farmhouse.
His advice is said to have helped settle a quarrel among the Confederates in 1481.

teile.einleitung: Lousonna was a Roman settlement on the shore of Lake Geneva. The present-day city of Lausanne grew out of it. Its remains lie in the Vidy district, where the International Olympic Committee now has its headquarters.
wichtigste: Lousonna is the Roman predecessor of Lausanne.
It lay in what is now the Vidy district on Lake Geneva.
Lousonna had a harbour on the lakeshore.
At its largest, an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people lived there.
From the late 3rd century people moved to a protected hill.
Today the IOC headquarters stands in Vidy.

abschnitte.text: **Lousonna** lay on the north shore of **Lake Geneva**, in what is now the Lausanne district of **Vidy**. The settlement was located between the mouths of the rivers Flon and Chamberonne. The name is recorded on old **inscriptions**. The present-day name **Lausanne** developed from it. The Romans called a settlement like this a **vicus**, that is, a village or a small town.

The position on the lake was very good for **trade**. There was a **harbour** on the shore. An inscription by boatmen shows that goods were transported across the water. Boats were often faster in those days than carts on the road. Important roads also ran past Lousonna.

The vicus was about **20 hectares** in size. At its largest, an estimated **1,500 to 2,000** people lived there. This made Lousonna one of the larger settlements in the land of the Helvetii. There were houses, workshops, a marketplace and temples. Parts of the walls can be seen today in a park.

From the late **3rd century** things became unsafe. Germanic groups carried out **raids** into the Roman Empire. So people moved further up to a protected place. There the medieval **bishop's city** of Lausanne with its cathedral later grew up. The old settlement by the lake fell into ruin.

Today Vidy is a district with parks on the lakeshore. In the **Musée romain** of Lausanne-Vidy you can look at finds from Lousonna. Vidy is also home to the **Olympic House**, the headquarters of the **International Olympic Committee**. It stands where parts of the Roman settlement once lay.

gewusst: The name Lausanne goes back to the Roman name Lousonna.
The headquarters of the Olympic movement stands on the site of a Roman settlement.

teile.einleitung: Louis Favre was a building contractor from the Geneva area. He led the construction of the Gotthard railway tunnel, one of the greatest building projects of his time. However, he did not live to see it finished.
wichtigste: Louis Favre was a building contractor.
He came from Chêne-Bourg near Geneva.
He led the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel.
In July 1879 he died during an inspection in the tunnel.
On 29 February 1880 the two teams of builders met inside the mountain.
Favre did not live to see the breakthrough.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Favre** came from **Chêne-Bourg** near Geneva. He was a **building contractor**, that is, someone who plans large construction work and carries it out with his workers. Before the Gotthard he had already built other tunnels. In 1872 he won the contract for the great tunnel at the Gotthard. He promised to finish the work in a short time.

The **Gotthard Tunnel** was to carry the railway from Göschenen in the canton of Uri to Airolo in Ticino. It is about 15 kilometres long. Work went on from both sides at the same time. The workers used **explosives** and drilling machines driven by compressed air. Many workers came from Italy. The work was hard and dangerous, and many workers lost their lives.

In July **1879** Louis Favre carried out an inspection in the tunnel. He suddenly felt unwell. Shortly afterwards he died of **heart failure**. The tunnel was not yet finished, and he did not live to see the end.

On **29 February 1880** the workers from the north and the south met inside the mountain. This moment is called the **breakthrough**. The two tunnels met each other very precisely. In 1882 the Gotthard Railway was opened. For the first time you could now travel by train under the Alps to the south.

gewusst: The breakthrough at the Gotthard took place on 29 February, in a leap year.
Louis Favre died in the tunnel he had built, only a few months before the breakthrough.

teile.einleitung: Matthäus Merian the Elder was a copper engraver and publisher from Basel. He drew hundreds of views of towns and cities. His pictures show us today what towns looked like almost 400 years ago.
wichtigste: Matthäus Merian was born in Basel in 1593.
He made his pictures as copper engravings.
He especially liked drawing views of towns and cities.
In 1615 he drew Basel from a bird's-eye view.
In Frankfurt he ran a publishing house.
His “Topographia” shows countries and towns.
His daughter Maria Sibylla became famous for her pictures of butterflies.

abschnitte.text: **Matthäus Merian** was born in **Basel** in **1593**. He learned the craft of **copper engraving**. Afterwards he travelled through various countries and worked in several towns. Later he settled in **Frankfurt**. There he spent most of his life.

In **copper engraving** you scratch a picture, in mirror image, into a smooth **copper plate**. Then you rub ink into the grooves. With a press you print the picture on paper. Many **prints** can be made from one plate. So Merian's pictures could be sold in large numbers.

In **1615** Merian drew a famous plan of Basel. It shows the city from a **bird's-eye view**, that is, as if you were flying over it like a bird. You can see all the houses, lanes, churches and the Rhine. The plan is very precise. It is an important record of old Basel.

Merian married into a **Frankfurt publishing family**. Soon he was running a **publishing house** himself. His greatest work is the **“Topographia”**. It is a large series of books with pictures and descriptions of towns and regions. There is also a volume on **Switzerland**. The texts were mostly written by the scholar Martin Zeiller.

Merian's daughter **Maria Sibylla Merian** became famous herself. She painted **caterpillars and butterflies** very precisely and even travelled to South America for this. Two sons also worked as artists. Many old houses and walls no longer exist today. On Merian's pictures you can still see them, so they are very **valuable** for history.

gewusst: Merian's pictures show towns as they looked in the 17th century.
His daughter Maria Sibylla Merian travelled to South America around 1700 to study butterflies.

teile.einleitung: In 1332 the city of Lucerne made an alliance with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. At that time Lucerne was under Habsburg rule. The alliance led to tensions and finally to the Sempach War.
wichtigste: In 1332 Lucerne allied itself with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
The alliance expressly reserved the rights of the Habsburgs.
In Lucerne there were tensions between friends of the alliance and circles loyal to the Habsburgs.
In 1385 the people of Lucerne destroyed the Habsburg castle of Rothenburg.
In 1386 the Confederates defeated Duke Leopold III at Sempach.
The Lucerne mayor Petermann von Gundoldingen fell in the battle.

abschnitte.text: In **1332** **Lucerne** made an alliance with the three forest cantons **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden**. At that time the city belonged to the **Habsburgs**. So the Habsburgs' rights as rulers were expressly **reserved** in the alliance. On paper, everything stayed as it was. In practice, though, the alliance weakened the Habsburgs' position in Lucerne.

Not everyone in Lucerne was in favour of the alliance. Part of the nobility and of the townspeople continued to side with the **rule of Austria**, that is, with the Habsburgs. Others wanted to work more closely with the forest cantons. For decades Lucerne was therefore torn between **two camps**. There were quarrels again and again.

North of the city the Habsburgs owned **Rothenburg** castle with a toll station. Anyone who brought goods past it had to pay **toll**. The people of Lucerne were very annoyed by this. In 1385 they destroyed the castle. This was an open challenge to the Habsburgs and helped to bring about the **Sempach War**.

In **1386** the **Battle of Sempach** took place. The Confederates defeated the army of **Duke Leopold III** of Austria. The duke fell in the fighting. The Lucerne **mayor Petermann von Gundoldingen** also died in the battle. He had led the people of Lucerne and was one of their most important politicians.

After the victory at Sempach, Lucerne was finally free of **Habsburg rule**. The city could now expand its territory greatly. It acquired many villages and districts in the surrounding area. Over time the present-day **canton of Lucerne** grew out of this.

gewusst: Lucerne was the first city to ally with the forest cantons.
At Sempach both leaders fell: Duke Leopold III and the Lucerne mayor Gundoldingen.

teile.einleitung: The Milan Wars were a series of wars over the rich Duchy of Milan around 1500. The Confederates fought in them as mercenaries and on their own account. In the end they lost at Marignano, but gained the area of present-day Ticino.
wichtigste: The Milan Wars were about the Duchy of Milan.
In 1500 Bellinzona passed to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.
In the Pavia Expedition of 1512 the Confederates drove the French out of Milan.
In 1513 the Confederates won at Novara.
In 1515 King Francis I of France defeated the Confederates at Marignano.
Cardinal Matthäus Schiner was an important opponent of France.
The Confederates gained the area of present-day Ticino.

abschnitte.text: Around 1500 the **Duchy of Milan** was one of the richest areas in Europe. France, the Habsburgs, Venice, the Pope and the Confederates all wanted influence there. The Confederates often fought as **mercenaries**, that is, for foreign lords in return for pay. Sometimes, though, they also fought on their own account. Swiss foot soldiers were considered very strong at that time.

In **1500** Swiss mercenaries stood on both sides. They served Duke **Ludovico Sforza** and also the French king. The mercenaries of Sforza refused to fight against their fellow countrymen. So Ludovico Sforza fell into **French captivity**. This is called the **“betrayal at Novara”**. In the same year **Bellinzona** with its three castles passed to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.

Cardinal **Matthäus Schiner**, Bishop of Sion, recruited Confederates against France on behalf of the Pope. In the **Pavia Expedition** of 1512 the Confederates drove the French out of Milan. They installed **Massimiliano Sforza**, the son of Ludovico, as duke. Milan was thus in effect a Confederate protectorate. In 1513 the Confederates defeated a French army at **Novara**.

In September **1515** the **Battle of Marignano** took place. The young French king **Francis I** had strong cavalry and many cannon. With the help of Venice he defeated the Confederates. **Ulrich Zwingli** was there as field preacher of the men of Glarus. His experiences later made him an opponent of mercenary service.

After Marignano the Confederates made **peace** with France in 1516. They gave up their plans for rule in northern Italy. But areas such as **Lugano** and **Locarno** remained in their possession. They were administered as **bailiwicks south of the Alps**. From these the canton of **Ticino** later developed.

gewusst: The three castles of Bellinzona are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Marignano is often seen as the end of the Confederates' policy of conquest.
